title: PGlite-backed analytics is about 1.36x the time of Postgres on 600+ real queries, so the memory store is a genuine alternative rather than a toy
content:
Because metrics collection is performance-sensitive, the analytics engine ships a benchmark suite comparing its store implementations, **run on every publish** with major-release results kept in the repository.

The headline: `MemoryAnalyticsStore` and `PostgresAnalyticsStore` are "very close in performance, with the Postgres implementation slightly faster in most applications."

**Query-list benchmark** — the 600+ most frequent real-world queries against matching tables of around **200k records**: on average the memory (PGlite) store took about **1.36×** the time of the Postgres store.

**WASM benchmark** — startup and insert cost for the memory store:

| Operation | Ops/sec | Average time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Init | 3 | 323.00 ms |
| 100 inserts | 478 | 2.08 ms |
| 200k inserts | 0 | 4448.10 ms |

Read together, those numbers say something useful about design choices: a **one-off 323 ms** initialisation and a 36% query penalty is a reasonable price for running the same analytics code in a browser with no server — which is exactly the trade the vault's own PGlite-based semantic search makes. The 200k-insert figure is the one to respect: bulk backfill into a WASM database is measured in seconds, so a processor replaying long history should expect it.
